newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION - Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup-Taxing troubles.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION - Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup-Taxing troubles.

text.p: By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)
Simmering for months, the flame has been turned up on the superannuation pot and it's spitting and spilling dangerous hot mix all over Peter Cosetllo's fair-go budget.
The so-called superannuation surcharge was one of the main initiatives which earned Cosetllo's first budget the "fair go" tag. It was perfect.
A revenue measure which hit only high income earners by carrying the progressivity of the tax system through to superannuation concessions.
Politically, it was also a beauty; virtually impossible for Labor and the Australian Democrats to block in the Senate.
And fiscally it was to deliver a sizeable wad of the consolidation task -- $480 million next financial year, A$470 million in 1998/99 and A$530 million in 1999/00.
But soon after the budget, the negatives began to surface. The superannuation funds, of course, began to raise their objections early.
The government chose to collect the surcharge through the super funds, rather than applying it directly to taxpayers' group certificates.

This had the advantage of distancing it from taxpayers, using the funds' structures to gather it, and making it less likely for the 'surcharge' to be criticised as a breach of the government's pre-election promise to introduce no new taxes, or raise existing ones.
The funds beat a path to Costello's door, complaining of the cumbersome nature of the collection method and its high cost. They ran into a brick wall.
The employer and industry groups joined the fray, pointing out that the 'surcharge' would significantly lessen the attractiveness of super for high income earners.

That's now been carried through to a survey by the Institute of Chartered Accountants showing 60 percent of clients were being advised to change their retirement planning to divert funds into property and, more particularly, into direct share investment to take advantage of tax-free fully imputed dividend incomes.
The institute summed up the fall-out: "The shift in funds that will occur shows that the government is unlikely to collect the A$480 million a year in revenue they are seeking.
"Superannuation has never been an attractive investment for low income earners. With the surcharge, the government has ensured that superannuation is not an attractive investment for anyone."

But that threat of a diminishing return from the surcharge this has been put in the shade by a bigger, darker cloud -- the very real prospect that the measure is unconstitutional and may not be collected at all until after that rather fundamental problem is addressed.
The development was all the more potent because the opinion was delivered by the federal government's former chief legal officer, Dennis Rose QC, now advising the Business Council.
"My preliminary view is that the supposed Superannuation Surcharge (Assessment and Collection) Act 1997, if enacted in the terms of the current bill would probably be wholly invalid," he said.
"Given the imposition of a tax on person A, it is not within those powers of the Commonwealth to require another person B to pay the amount of the tax to the Commonwealth."
That claimed breach was caused by the government's insistence on the funds paying the surcharge (according to the government) or the tax, (according to just about everyone else, including Mr Rose).
Manna from heaven for the opposition. Labor has not been able to oppose the tax outright because it would appear to be trying to block an equity measure.
But it could certainly move amendments to a bill declared unconstitutional by a highly-respected QC.
In fact, most opponents of the current bill do not object to the concept of the tax, rather than the method of its collection.
Everyone from the super funds outwards have been telling the government to adopt the group certificate route and all the problems will be solved.

The government's rejected all advances. This week, this was escalated with the prime minister declaring the funds to be acting solely out of self-interest in trying to "destroy" the fair measure, putting the funds on the same level as the party.
If John Howard's design was to increase the likelihood of a High Court challenge, he's succeeded.
The cost to the funds of the surcharge/tax is big and would be ongoing. That alone justifies the expense of a challenge.

There's a more immediate threat. Four states -- New South Wales, South Australia, Queensland and Western Australia -- have threatened not to co-operate; that is, not to collect the tax from their own employees.
The states argue too that the bill is unconstitutional because the commonwealth may not tax the property of the states. Even Costello has admitted that design fault.

But there's more politicking in the states stance. They know that rejecting the surcharge outright might have a political cost, by appearing to set their public servants above the rest of the community. The more likely outcome is that the states will continue their threats until the Commonwealth agrees to some compensation for the costs of collection.
Nevertheless, the surcharge will be another volatile ingredient in the fractious premiers' conference next Friday.
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
